No, 3M does not look especially capital-intensive on FY2022 data. Capital spending was $1,749M in 2022 (up from $1,603M in 2021) and net PP&E was $9,178M. The pages do not give FY2022 net sales or total assets, so a precise capex/sales or PP&E/assets ratio can't be computed from them. Capex of about $1.7B is modest relative to a large global manufacturer with roughly 92,000 employees and about $9.2B of net PP&E, so 3M is a moderately asset-heavy manufacturer rather than a highly capital-intensive business. This is a qualitative judgment, not a ratio-based conclusion.

The latest year covered is FY2021 (operating margin down 1.5 points, or 0.5 points to 20.8% excluding special items, driven by COVID-related raw material/logistics cost increases and supply chain challenges, partly offset by productivity and restructuring savings). Operating margin is a useful metric for 3M, which uses operating income as a primary segment performance measure and reconciles margin changes each year, but no FY2022 figures are available here.

The retrieved pages do not include 3M's Q2 2023 balance sheet line items (accounts receivable and the split of current vs. long-term marketable securities), so an exact quick ratio cannot be computed from them. The quick ratio is a relevant liquidity measure for 3M, but these pages cannot support a precise figure. What they do show points to adequate but not exceptional liquidity at June 30, 2023. Current ratio: $15,754M current assets / $10,936M current liabilities = about 1.44x, with working capital of $4,818M, down $347M from year-end 2022. Cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities were $4,337M, so cash-only coverage of current liabilities is at most about 0.40x. Adding receivables (not given here) would raise the quick ratio, but inventory is a large part of current assets, so it would likely stay below the 1.44x current ratio. Liquidity is also supported by an undrawn $4.25B revolving credit facility, $1.8B of commercial paper outstanding against a $5B program, and an EBITDA-to-interest covenant ratio of about 17:1 against a 3.0:1 minimum. Credit outlooks are negative (Moody's A2 negative, S&P A- CreditWatch negative), so the profile is reasonably healthy but weakening.

As of Q2 2023 (10-Q for the quarter ended June 30, 2023), three 3M debt securities are registered under Section 12(b) and listed on the New York Stock Exchange: the 1.500% Notes due 2026 (ticker MMM26), the 1.750% Notes due 2030 (MMM30), and the 1.500% Notes due 2031 (MMM31).

Yes. 3M has paid dividends since 1916 and raised them every year through the period covered. Dividends paid per share rose from $4.10 (2015) to $4.44 (2016), $4.70 (2017), $5.44 (2018), $5.76 (2019) and $5.88 (2020). The annual rate was then set at $5.92 (Feb 2021) and $6.00 (Feb 2023, +1%), and the Feb 2023 increase marked the 65th consecutive year of increases. Total cash dividends paid grew from $2.561B in 2015 to $3.388B in 2020. The pace of increase varied (16% in Jan 2018 vs. 1% in 2021 and 2023), and the Q2 2023 dividend was held at $1.50, but the trend is steady and rising.

Yes. Free cash flow conversion (FCF = operating cash flow minus purchases of property and equipment, divided by net income) rose each year through FY2022. FY2020: (5,727-419)/5,260 = 5,308/5,260, about 101%. FY2021: (7,230-348)/4,822 = 6,882/4,822, about 143%. FY2022: (7,838-442)/4,756 = 7,396/4,756, about 156%. Conversion improved from about 143% in FY2021 to about 156% in FY2022, because operating cash flow grew while net income was slightly lower. As a share of revenue, FCF conversion cannot be checked from these pages because they do not include FY2022 revenue.

Roughly 12 times in FY2022, but this is a derived approximation and the ratio is of limited meaning for AES. The pages do not give FY2022 cost of sales directly. I estimated it as revenue minus operating margin, since AES's operating margin is revenue less cost of sales. Quarterly revenue sums to $12,617M (2,852+3,078+3,627+3,060) and operating margin to $2,548M (530+563+892+563), so cost of sales is about $10,069M. Average inventory is ($1,055M at 2022 year-end + $604M at 2021 year-end)/2 = $829.5M. Turnover is about 10,069/829.5 ≈ 12.1x, or about 30 days of inventory. Conventional inventory management is not very meaningful for AES because it is a power generator and utility. Its inventory is mainly fuel and other raw materials ($733M) and spare parts and supplies ($322M), held to keep plants running, not goods bought for resale. Its cost of sales also includes non-inventory costs such as purchased power and depreciation, so the ratio is only a rough indicator.

Amcor primarily operates in the global packaging industry. It develops and produces responsible packaging (flexible and rigid packaging, specialty cartons, closures) for food, beverage, pharmaceutical, medical, home and personal-care, and other consumer goods end markets, organized into two segments: Flexibles and Rigid Packaging.

No. Amcor's gross margin deteriorated through FY2023 rather than improving: 21.2% (FY2021) -> 19.4% (FY2022) -> 18.5% (FY2023), with gross profit of $2,725M in FY2023 vs $2,820M in FY2022 (-3%). It was also falling in earlier years (21.0% in FY2017, 19.9% in FY2018, 19.0% in FY2019). Gross margin is also of limited use for Amcor, because raw material cost increases are passed through to customers as higher net sales (about $776M in FY2023). This inflates the sales denominator and mechanically lowers the percentage even when dollar profit holds up. Excluding currency and disposed operations, gross profit rose $56M in FY2023 on better operating cost performance. A better gauge is Adjusted EBIT in dollars and as a percentage of sales, which Amcor itself says carries about 90 bps of adverse pass-through impact in FY2023. Adjusted EBIT margin fell from 11.7% to 10.9%, so that measure did not improve either.

As of December 31, 2022 (end of Q2 FY2023), Amcor's restructuring liability was $93 million (employee costs $81M, fixed-asset related costs $2M, other costs $10M). It is an accrual for restructuring activities, primarily tied to the Russia-Ukraine conflict (the earlier 2019 Bemis integration plan was substantially completed at the end of FY2022). The liability is made up mainly of employee-related costs such as severance, with smaller amounts for fixed-asset related and other costs. It is recorded in other current and other non-current liabilities, and the majority is expected to be paid within the next twelve months.
Amcor's adjusted non-GAAP EBITDA for fiscal 2023 (twelve months ended June 30, 2023) was $2,018 million, down 5% from $2,117 million in fiscal 2022 (up 1% on a comparable constant currency basis).

The real change in Amcor's net sales in FY2023 vs FY2022, excluding FX, pass-through of raw material costs and one-off items (disposed and ceased operations), was an increase of $7 million (0%). Reported net sales rose $150 million, from $14,544M to $14,694M. The adjustments were pass-through of raw material costs of $776M, negative currency impact of $426M and negative impact of disposed/ceased operations of $207M. As of FY22, AMD sells: (1) for data centers, server CPUs (EPYC), GPUs (Instinct accelerators), DPUs (from Pensando), FPGAs and Adaptive SoCs; (2) for PCs, client CPUs and APUs (Ryzen, Ryzen PRO, Threadripper, Athlon) and chipsets for desktop and notebook; (3) discrete GPUs (Radeon, Radeon PRO) plus semi-custom SoCs and development services (game consoles such as PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, Steam Deck); and (4) embedded CPUs, GPUs, APUs, FPGAs (Virtex, Kintex, Artix, Spartan) and Adaptive SoCs (Zynq, Versal), plus Alveo acceleration boards and Vivado/Vitis software. AMD may also sell or license portions of its IP. The Xilinx (Feb 2022) and Pensando (May 2022) acquisitions added the FPGA, Adaptive SoC and DPU lines.

AMD's FY2022 net revenue rose 44% to $23.6B from $16.4B in 2021. Drivers: Data Center revenue +64% (to $6.0B) on higher EPYC server processor sales; Gaming +21% (to $6.8B) on higher semi-custom sales; Embedded jumped from $246M to $4.55B due to the Xilinx acquisition. Partly offset by a 10% decline in Client revenue (to $6.2B) from lower processor shipments (-24% units) amid a weak PC market and inventory corrections.

The pages do not include AMD's FY2022 10-K, so FY22 operating margin and its drivers cannot be determined from them. The closest available data is AMD's FY2021 vs FY2020 (the prior-year comparison). Operating margin is a meaningful metric for AMD. In FY21, revenue rose to $16,434M from $9,763M, and gross margin improved to 48% from 45% on a richer mix of EPYC, Radeon and Ryzen. R&D rose to $2,845M from $1,983M and MG&A to $1,448M from $995M. Segment operating income rose strongly, which suggests higher revenue and margin more than offset higher operating expenses. Computing and Graphics operating income was $2.1B vs $1.3B, and Enterprise, Embedded and Semi-Custom was $2.0B vs $391M. This is not FY22 data.

As of 2022, American Express reports its geographic operations in four regions plus the U.S.: the United States (the largest, $41,396M of $52,862M total 2022 revenues net of interest expense), EMEA (Europe, Middle East and Africa; $4,871M), APAC (Asia Pacific, Australia and New Zealand; $3,835M) and LACC (Latin America, Canada and the Caribbean; $2,917M). Outside the U.S., the jurisdictions representing a significant portion of billed business are the UK, the EU, Australia, Japan, Canada and Mexico.

Operating margin is not a useful metric for American Express, and the provided pages do not show an operating margin trend for it. AmEx is a card issuer and payments network, and its income statement does not report an operating income or operating margin line. Revenue is reported net of interest expense, and large provisions for credit losses are part of core operations. In 2022 the provision swung from a $2.5 billion reserve release in 2021 to a $617 million reserve build. Net income fell to $7.5 billion from $8.1 billion even though total revenues net of interest expense grew 25%. So 2022 profitability is better read through net income, EPS ($9.85 vs. $10.02), revenue growth, and credit metrics, and on those it was not an improving margin year.

Gross margin is not a meaningful or reported metric for American Express, so there is no FY2022 gross margin change to attribute. As a payments and lending company, American Express has no cost of goods sold. Its revenues are discount revenue, net card fees, and net interest income, and its main costs are interest expense, provisions for credit losses, Card Member rewards, and operating expenses. The retrieved pages contain no AmEx gross margin figure; the gross margin discussions in them are for other companies (Apple, Costco, Corning). The closest relevant FY2022 driver is net interest income, which rose $2,145 million versus 2021: interest income rose $3,625 million (volume +$2,287 million, rate +$1,338 million), mainly on Card Member loans, while interest expense rose $1,480 million, mostly from higher rates on savings deposits and long-term debt.

American Express's effective tax rate fell from 24.6% in FY2021 to 21.6% in FY2022, a decrease of 3.0 percentage points, primarily due to discrete tax benefits in 2022 from the resolution of prior-year tax items.

The largest liability on American Express's consolidated balance sheet at December 31, 2022 was Customer deposits at $110,239 million (about 54% of total liabilities of $203,643 million). It exceeded Long-term debt ($42,573 million), Other liabilities ($37,350 million), Accounts payable ($12,133 million) and Short-term borrowings ($1,348 million).

Yes. Amex says Card Member retention remained high in 2022, and its card base grew: proprietary cards-in-force rose 7% to 76.7 million (from 71.4 million) and total cards-in-force rose 10% to 133.3 million. Net card fees grew 17% as record new acquisitions combined with high retention.

No. American Water Works did not have positive working capital at FY2022 year-end. The 2022 10-K risk factors state that as of December 31, 2022 its working capital (current assets less current liabilities) was in a deficit position. The MD&A explains this is normal for the company: current liabilities may exceed current assets mainly because of debt maturities due within one year and the use of short-term debt (commercial paper) to fund maturities, acquisitions and construction. It manages the timing gaps through short-term liquidity mechanisms, such as a $2.75 billion revolving credit facility with $1.50 billion available. So a working capital deficit is structural for this capital-intensive regulated utility and is not a strong sign of distress, which makes the metric less informative than liquidity and cash flow measures. The balance sheet figures were not in the provided pages, so I cannot give the exact dollar deficit. The cash flow statement shows changes in working capital of $(355) million in 2022, which is a cash outflow and not the balance.

Yes, three segments exceeded 20% of FY2022 revenue of $66,608M: Commercial Airplanes at $25,867M (about 38.8%), Defense, Space & Security at $23,162M (about 34.8%), and Global Services at $17,611M (about 26.4%). Boeing Capital ($199M, about 0.3%) is far below the threshold.

Yes. Boeing's FY2022 10-K (Note 21) discloses two main ongoing legal matters. (1) 737 MAX litigation: multiple legal actions remain pending from the Lion Air Flight 610 (Oct 2018) and Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302 (Mar 2019) accidents. The 2021 DOJ Deferred Prosecution Agreement and a shareholder derivative settlement (Boeing received $219 million in Q2 2022) are resolved, and the SEC investigation was settled in Sept 2022 with a $200 million civil penalty paid in Oct 2022. Boeing cannot reasonably estimate a range of loss, if any, not covered by insurance from the remaining pending lawsuits. (2) Embraer arbitration: Boeing terminated the 2019 agreements in 2020 (it was to acquire 80% of Embraer's commercial aircraft business for $4,200 million). Embraer disputes the termination and the dispute is in arbitration, expected to conclude in late 2023 or early 2024, with no reasonably estimable range of loss. The 10-K also warns generally that litigation and government investigations could materially affect results.

No clear improvement, and gross margin is not a very useful metric for Boeing. The provided pages do not include the income statement with revenue and cost of sales for FY2022, so a gross margin trend cannot be computed. Boeing's own disclosures focus on program-level gross margins and operating margins because it uses program accounting and long-term contract accounting, so cost of sales and margins are driven by judgmental estimates, reach-forward losses and cumulative catch-up adjustments (e.g., $3.5B 787 loss in Q4 2021, abnormal production costs of $2.8B estimated). At Dec 31, 2022 the 767, 777X and 787 programs had near break-even or single-digit margins, and cumulative abnormal 787 costs were $1.7B. BDS operating margin fell from 5.8% in 2021 to (15.3)% in 2022. Consolidated operating margins were negative in 2021 (-4.7%) after -22.0% in 2020, but the pages give no consolidated 2022 figure. Overall, the evidence shows thin program margins and volatile, estimate-driven results rather than a clearly improving gross margin profile; operating margin and program margins are the more meaningful measures.

The pages do not include Boeing's FY2022 10-K Business section, so FY2022 customer data is not directly shown. The most recent filings (FY2021, with the same description in FY2020 and FY2019) show Boeing's primary customers are: commercial airlines worldwide (BCA, plus BGS commercial services); the U.S. Department of Defense (BDS' primary customer, about 84% of BDS 2021 revenues, including foreign military sales through the U.S. government); and other significant BDS customers such as NASA and international defense, civil and commercial satellite customers. The FY2022 10-K overview page confirms the same business mix (commercial jetliners for the worldwide commercial airline industry and one of the largest U.S. defense contractors, with airline customers in North and South America, the Middle East and Europe). U.S. government revenue was 89% of BDS revenue in 2021.

Yes. Boeing's 10-K risk factors state that demand for its commercial aircraft and services depends on the airline industry, which "traditionally ... has been cyclical and very competitive and has experienced significant profit swings." Economic or industry downturns could lead to fewer orders, postponed or cancelled contracts, lower revenues, profitability and cash flows, and a smaller backlog. The language appears in the 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020 and 2021 10-Ks.

Per Boeing's FY2022 10-K, for 2023 Boeing expects: 787 to gradually increase from low rates to 5 per month; 777X-9 production, paused during 2022 and 2023, to resume in 2023; and 737 to gradually increase above the current 31 per month based on market demand and supply chain capacity (no specific 2023 target given). What they show: cash and cash equivalents were only $2.6 billion at Dec 31, 2022, while about $9.3 billion of debt, $4.6 billion of operating leases, $4.8 billion of C-Band commitments and $9.4 billion of purchase obligations fall due within 12 months. That suggests a quick ratio well below 1.0 on a cash-only basis. However, the quick ratio is of limited relevance for Verizon: it is a capital-intensive, recurring-revenue telecom that funds obligations mainly from operating cash flow ($37.1 billion in 2022) and external financing (commercial paper, credit facilities, debt issuance, asset-backed receivables monetization), and management states its sources of funds are sufficient for the next 12 months and beyond. Liquidity is therefore better judged by operating cash flow and financing access than by a quick ratio.
